newsitem.title: MEXICO: FOCUS-Freezes may shrink 96-97 Mexico coffee crop.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Freezes may shrink 96-97 Mexico coffee crop.

text.p: Mexico's 1996-1997 coffee production could fall by 20 to 30 percent from the previous cycle because of poor weather, with output in some states dropping by 40 percent, growers and traders told Reuters on Wednesday.
"The national average is expected to fall 20 to 30 percent (from last year's crop)," said Juan Carlos Villareal, executive director of the Confederation of Mexican Coffee Growers.

A drop of about 10 percent from last year's bumper crop had been expected because of normal seasonal fluxes, Mexican coffee associations recently have further lowered their crop estimates for the 1996-97 cycle.
In the 1995-1996 season about five million 60-kg bags of coffee were produced in Mexico, with exports of 4.58 million bags.

Coffee associations said they had not yet calculated precise damage to the 1996-1997 crop or next year's coffee because of past months' frosts and drought. The crop is just entering peak harvest season, typically the first three months of the year.
"The harvest is coming in really bad, possibly up to 40 percent lower than last year," Puebla state farmer Pablo Gomez said. "The cold has hit us hard."
"We saw in Veracruz that production was expected to drop but in Chiapas it would rise. Now the volume in Chiapas doesn't look so good," said a coffee trader who declined to be identified.
A lack of rains hurt Chiapas, Mexico's top coffee-producing state. Then freezing temperatures in December and January damaged plants at higher altitudes in Veracruz and Puebla states.

After a recent trip to Hidalgo, Mexico's sixth-largest coffee-producing state, the trader said coffee was coming in frozen and burnt, "a brown color rather than the usual green." Such damage is irreversible and unpreventable, he said. About 40 percent of the state's crops, which totalled 149,630 bags in the 1994-1995 season, have been reported destroyed.

But other coffee experts say low coffee prices and less government and private financing for farmers restricted planting and exacerbated damage done by Mother Nature. "There are various factors, principally the lack of resources and attention to the plantations," the confederation's Villareal said.

"Also it is related to lower-than-hoped-for prices and the danger that prices would continue falling," said Luis Hernandez, spokesman for the National Coordinating Council of Coffee Organizations. The organization represents the country's largest group of small farmers.
